extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students handling injunctions and validity disputes in U.S. federal courts
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules for treating prior judicial judgments as proof of patent validity on motions for preliminary injunctions and related preliminary relief in U.S. patent litigation. Covers the weight and effect of Supreme Court, Circuit court, and other decisions, modes of hearing, consent/collusive decrees, reissues, and when de novo hearings are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court decisions binding as plenary proof of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States is binding on all other courts until reversed or modified; its decision that a patent is valid must be received as plenary proof of such validity between the same parties and on the same issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption can be overcome only by showing the Supreme Court judgment was obtained by fraud or that newly discovered evidence, if presented at the former trial, would have produced a different result. On questions of interpretation or definition the Supreme Court's judgment must be followed even though the parties may be different. Supreme Court determinations are entitled to the highest deference because of the wide research and careful scrutiny by which they are preceded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for granting preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue when the novelty of the invention is established; when the patent has been sustained after a full hearing and the infringement is clear; and especially where the very form of the device used by the defendant has been passed upon in a former case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are more willing to grant preliminary relief when the patent's novelty and validity have already been judicially sustained and when infringement is apparent; the defendant's willingness to give security is relevant. Examples cited: Hussey v. Whitely; Conover v. Mers. A preliminary injunction carries less weight than a final decree, however.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior adjudication on reissued patents
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjudication on an original patent is not a ground for an injunction on a reissue where the reissue claims are different, or where the reissue is broader than the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reissue attempts to broaden coverage beyond the original patent, prior adjudication of the original does not automatically support an injunction on the reissue. Also, if the Supreme Court has held the original patent invalid, an injunction on the reissue will generally not be granted as if it were a new valid patent. Cases: Poppenhusen v. Falke; Wells v. Jacquet; Jones v. McMurray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit court judgments as sufficient evidence of validity (same circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment in the Circuit court of the same circuit sustaining a patent between the same parties and upon the same issues is sufficient evidence of validity for purposes of a subsequent injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where parties differ, the value of the judgment depends on the nature of the questions decided and the thoroughness of consideration. Circuit-court decisions within the same circuit raise a strong presumption in favor of the patent and are generally followed on motions for injunction unless new evidence or a change in controlling law would lead to a different result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial construction by one court usually followed by others
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial construction given to a patent by one court will usually be followed in another court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior constructions have persuasive weight because courts seek consistency; however, constructions are not necessarily final and may be reinterpreted in different contexts. See Consolidated Safety Valve Co. v. Kunkle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions conclusive only between same parties and privies
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions in former cases offered to prove priority or validity are not conclusive except between the same parties and their privies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision sustaining a patent between certain parties creates a strong presumption of validity as to them, but that presumption does not automatically bind unrelated parties in a different litigation; see Day v. Combination Rubber Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-party to former suit entitled to de novo hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant was not a party to the former suit, he is entitled to a hearing de novo on an application for injunctive relief, though past decisions on the same facts have considerable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-parties can present fresh evidence and arguments; past adjudications are influential but do not foreclose reconsideration. Example: Page v. Holmes Burglar Alarm Telegraph Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of judgments varies with mode of adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree based on a full hearing by a court (final hearing) is of greater weight than one based on a jury verdict, a feigned issue, or a hearing before a master; a decision on an application for a preliminary injunction is of less weight than a final decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final judicial consideration with full hearing, careful deliberation, and examination of law and fact provides the strongest evidence of validity. Conversely, collusive or consent decrees, verdicts on feigned issues, or dismissals for failure to prove infringement carry less or no weight in subsequent suits unless circumstances show acquiescence or absence of defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent decrees and their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree by consent, if without collusion, binds the defendant in the same circuit but has no effect on other parties nor against him in other circuits unless his surrender resulted from his knowledge of lacking an adequate defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent decrees demonstrate acquiescence of the defendant in that decision and can be binding between the same parties; however, they do not create universal res judicata against different parties or in different circuits. Examples: Tomkinson v. Willetts Mfg. Co.; United States & Foreign Salamander Felting Co. v. Asbestos Felting Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collusive decrees have no value
rubrics_metrics.description: Collusive decrees are of no value against any party and are not a ground for an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A suit is collusive if, for example, one party pays counsel fees on both sides; such decrees will be disregarded. Courts scrutinize the mode in which conclusions were attained to detect collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-circuit authority and comity
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment of a Circuit court in another circuit has no controlling authority, but comity gives such judgments weight measured by character, number, eminence of judges, and care with which questions were considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not binding, decisions from other circuits—especially where multiple circuits have reached the same conclusion after careful consideration—are persuasive and courts often follow them to avoid conflicting constructions of patents. Where the same points are repeatedly adjudicated without appeal, the cumulative persuasive force is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis subject to correction: reconsideration only in special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines once established will not be reconsidered except in special cases where justice requires it; courts adhere to prior decisions unless there is a clear mistake, newly discovered testimony, or questions not previously considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will follow co-ordinate tribunals' decisions on issues of law or construction unless good reason exists to depart. The rule of comity and the desire to avoid shifting rules supports adherence, but flexibility remains when justice or newly discovered evidence demands review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative weight of multiple sustaining judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrence of judgments in different courts (e.g., several Circuit courts) sustaining the patent, particularly after full hearings covering conceivable objections, creates a strong or almost conclusive presumption of validity for purposes of an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple courts have sustained a patent after careful adjudication—and especially if four judgments sustain the patent or several circuits have ruled similarly—the courts will treat the patent as valid for preliminary relief purposes unless new features are presented or the Supreme Court reverses. Examples: statements about four judgments or multiple circuit acquiescence in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weight: final decree v. preliminary ruling and jury verdicts
rubrics_metrics.description: A final decree on the merits (after a full hearing) carries more weight and is better evidence of validity than a decision on a motion for a preliminary injunction or a jury verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions after full hearings, particularly by equity courts or judges experienced in patent law, are more authoritative. A dismissal for failure to prove infringement is not necessarily a bar to another suit; verdicts on feigned issues or hearings before masters are weaker evidence.
